If You Only Remember These

~20 facts that unlock everything else. Read this twice before you read anything else.
  • 30S = AT, 50S = CELL. Aminoglycosides & Tetracyclines hit the 30S subunit. Chloramphenicol, Erythromycin (macrolides), Linezolid, Lincosamides (clindamycin) hit the 50S subunit.
  • Beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, monobactams, carbapenems) inhibit transpeptidases (PBPs) → block peptidoglycan cross-linking → cell swells → bursts. Bactericidal, work best on actively dividing bacteria.
  • 4 ways bacteria evade beta-lactams: Destroy the drug (β-lactamase) · Change the target (altered PBP, e.g. PBP2a/mecA in MRSA) · Keep the drug out (porin loss) · Pump the drug out (efflux).
  • Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala directly (not PBPs) → blocks transglycosylation + transpeptidation. Resistance = D-Ala-D-Lac swap (VRE/VRSA), loses 1 H-bond, 1000-fold less binding.
  • Aminoglycosides are bactericidal, 30S, need oxygen-dependent active transport to get in → useless against anaerobes. Concentration-dependent killing + long post-antibiotic effect → once-daily dosing.
  • Tetracyclines are bacteriostatic, reversibly block the 30S A-site (aminoacyl-tRNA can't dock). Avoid <8 years old and pregnancy (teeth/bone).
  • Macrolides/Clindamycin/Chloramphenicol/Linezolid all converge on the 50S subunit but each blocks a different step (translocation, peptidyl transferase, or 70S initiation).
  • Chloramphenicol = aplastic anemia (idiosyncratic, dose-independent) + reversible marrow suppression (dose-dependent) + gray baby syndrome (no UDP-glucuronyl transferase in neonates).
  • Clindamycin = best anaerobic coverage above the diaphragm + suppresses toxin production (necrotizing fasciitis/TSS) but #1 cause tied to C. difficile colitis.
  • Linezolid blocks 70S initiation complex assembly, covers MRSA/VRE, 100% oral bioavailability, but causes thrombocytopenia, serotonin syndrome (MAO inhibitor), and optic/peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use.
  • Sulfonamides mimic PABA → block dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS). Trimethoprim mimics folate → blocks dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). Together = sequential blockade = bactericidal (each alone is bacteriostatic).
  • Selective toxicity of antifolates: bacteria must make their own folate (no transporter); mammals just absorb dietary folate. That is the entire reason these drugs are safe.
  • Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase (Gram-negatives) and topoisomerase IV (Gram-positives) → trap the DNA-enzyme complex → lethal double-strand breaks. Rapidly bactericidal.
  • Moxifloxacin is hepatically cleared, not renally → does NOT reach therapeutic urine levels → never use for UTI.
  • Cephalosporin generation trend: 1st = Gram + → 5th = adds MRSA, with exceptions to memorize: ceftazidime and cefepime cover Pseudomonas; ceftriaxone/ceftaroline/moxifloxacin do NOT.
  • Carbapenems = broadest spectrum "big guns." Imipenem needs cilastatin (blocks renal dehydropeptidase-1, prevents nephrotoxic metabolites + seizure risk). Ertapenem lacks Pseudomonas/Acinetobacter/enterococcus coverage.
  • Aztreonam (monobactam) = Gram-negative aerobes ONLY, no cross-allergy with penicillin/cephalosporins EXCEPT ceftazidime (identical side chain).
  • Classic "no coverage" list: Aminoglycosides = no anaerobes · Aztreonam = no Gram+/anaerobes · Vancomycin/linezolid/daptomycin = no Gram-negatives · Daptomycin = no pneumonia (inactivated by surfactant) · Metronidazole = no aerobes.
  • Red man syndrome (vancomycin) is NOT a true allergy — it's rate-related histamine release. Fix = slow the infusion, not stop the drug forever.
  • High-risk toxicity pairings to know cold: Aminoglycosides/vancomycin → nephro + ototoxicity · Fluoroquinolones → tendon rupture + QTc + CNS · Sulfonamides → SJS/TEN + G6PD hemolysis + kernicterus · Linezolid → thrombocytopenia + serotonin syndrome.

how the whole lecture fits together Every drug class in this trans attacks one of 5 targets: (1) cell wall (beta-lactams, vancomycin), (2) cell membrane (daptomycin), (3) 30S or 50S ribosome (protein synthesis inhibitors), (4) folate synthesis (sulfonamides/trimethoprim), or (5) DNA replication (fluoroquinolones). If you can name the target, you can usually derive the mechanism, and the toxicity pattern (organ toxicity, hypersensitivity, or superinfection) is what the exam actually tests.

I. Beta-Lactams

Penicillins · Cephalosporins · Monobactam · Carbapenems. All are cell-wall synthesis inhibitors sharing one core mechanism (PBP/transpeptidase inhibition) with different spectrums.
Penicillins Pages 1–2, 5 Must Know ▼
Mechanism of action (Molecular Mimicry → Lethal Cascade)
Beta-lactam ring structurally mimics the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursor
↓
Penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs = transpeptidases) bind the drug instead of the real substrate
↓
Stable covalent (irreversible) complex forms → PBP inactivated → no cross-linking
↓
Autolysins (murein hydrolases) keep degrading existing wall, unopposed
↓
Cell becomes hyperosmotic → water rushes in → cell swells → bursts (bactericidal)
Must know
  • Works best against actively dividing bacteria (need active cell-wall synthesis to be vulnerable)
  • Classification by property: Acid-resistant = Penicillin V · Penicillinase-resistant = Methicillin, Cloxacillin · Extended-spectrum = Amoxicillin, Ampicillin, Carbenicillin, Piperacillin · Beta-lactamase inhibitors = Clavulanic acid, Sulbactam, Tazobactam
  • Natural penicillins (Pen G IV, Pen V oral) → strep, meningococci, spirochetes (syphilis). Highly susceptible to beta-lactamase.
  • Anti-staphylococcal (Nafcillin, Oxacillin, Dicloxacillin) → bulky side chain sterically shields the ring → MSSA only, NOT MRSA.
  • Extended-spectrum: Aminopenicillins (Ampicillin, Amoxicillin) add some Gram-negative cover; Antipseudomonal (Piperacillin) covers Pseudomonas. Often paired with a beta-lactamase inhibitor.
  • Beta-lactamase inhibitors (clavulanic acid, sulbactam, tazobactam) are "suicide inhibitors" — weak antibacterial activity alone, irreversibly inactivate Class A beta-lactamases. Augmentin = amoxicillin-clavulanate, Unasyn = ampicillin-sulbactam, Zosyn = piperacillin-tazobactam.
  • Hypersensitivity is the major toxicity: mild rash → anaphylaxis (~0.05%). Penicilloic acid + host protein = hapten antigen.
Should know
  • Kinetics: 10% glomerular filtration + 90% active tubular secretion → half-life <1 hour. Probenecid blocks tubular secretion → prolongs half-life (used deliberately).
  • Biliary clearance exceptions: Nafcillin (no renal adjustment needed), Oxacillin (both routes).
  • Excellent penetration into pleural/pericardial/peritoneal/synovial fluid. Ceftriaxone/cefotaxime cross an inflamed BBB (that's cephalosporins, noted here for contrast).
  • High-dose neurotoxicity/seizures, especially with renal dysfunction (drug accumulation).
  • Organ-specific: Nafcillin → neutropenia · Oxacillin → hepatitis · Methicillin → acute interstitial nephritis (obsolete clinically, now used as the eponym for MRSA).
Nice to know
  • R-group table: Penicillin G (parenteral, G+ and a few G−), Penicillin V (oral, similar to G), Ampicillin (oral/parenteral, more G−), Amoxicillin (oral, better bioavailability than ampicillin), Methicillin (parenteral, G+ only incl. beta-lactamase producers).
Exam trap
An aminopenicillin rash is very commonly seen with concurrent EBV (mono) infection and does NOT necessarily mean true penicillin allergy — but don't casually reframe a reported "penicillin allergy" without proper allergy history-taking.
What does penicillin actually bind, and what happens instead of normal transpeptidation?
It binds PBPs (transpeptidases) by mimicking D-Ala-D-Ala, forming a stable covalent (irreversible) complex instead of completing cross-linking — functionally inactivating the enzyme.
Cephalosporins Pages 2–4 Must Know ▼
Must know
  • General trend: higher generation = more Gram-negative coverage, with important exceptions (memorize these, they are exam favorites).
Table 5. Cephalosporin generations
GenerationDrugsSpectrum focusKey use / landmark
1stCefazolin (IV), Cephalexin (oral)Gram-positive, minimal Gram-neg, inactive vs MRSAGold standard surgical prophylaxis, skin infections
2ndCefuroxime, Cefoxitin, Cefotetan, CefaclorExpanded Gram-neg (H. influenzae); cefoxitin/cefotetan add anaerobes (B. fragilis)Abdominal/pelvic surgical prophylaxis, upper resp infections
3rdCeftriaxone, Cefotaxime, CeftazidimeMassive Gram-neg, crosses BBB; ceftazidime = PseudomonasEmpirical meningitis, CAP, gonorrhea (ceftriaxone)
4thCefepime (IV)Ultra-broad: Gram+, Gram−, Pseudomonas; resistant to AmpCNosocomial infections, febrile neutropenia
5thCeftaroline fosamil (IV)Anti-MRSA (high affinity for altered PBP2a) + broad Gram-neg (~3rd gen)Complicated skin/soft tissue infection, CAP, MRSA
Mnemonic (Lecturer's mnemonic)1st = FA/PH (ceFAzolin, cePHAlexin — except Cefaclor) · 3rd = ONE/TEN/IME (ceftriaxONE, ceftibuTEN, cefotaxIME — except cefuroxime, which is 2nd) · 4th = PI (cefePIme) · 5th = ROL (ceftaROLine) · 2nd = everything else.
Mechanism of action
Same target class as penicillin: binds PBPs, inhibits transpeptidases
↓
Promotes autolysis (unopposed murein hydrolases)
↓
Increases cell-wall deficiency (CWD) → bactericidal lysis
Must know
  • Cross-allergy with penicillin ~5–10%. Contraindicated if history of severe immediate (anaphylactic) penicillin hypersensitivity.
  • Ceftriaxone exceptions to know: (1) biliary excretion, no renal adjustment; (2) displaces bilirubin → kernicterus risk, avoid in neonates; (3) precipitates with calcium → biliary pseudolithiasis.
  • MTT ring (Cefotetan, Cefamandole) → inhibits Vitamin K synthesis → bleeding risk + severe disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
  • Resistance: change in PBP affinity/structure, beta-lactamase production, decreased cell-wall permeability.
Should know
  • Structural modification at position 7 of the beta-lactam ring (via amidases) changes potency, efficacy, PK.
  • Indications beyond "alternative to penicillin": UTIs, soft tissue infection, septicemia, gonorrhea, typhoid, mixed aerobic/anaerobic infection, surgical prophylaxis.
  • Side effects: injection-site pain, thrombophlebitis, diarrhea, hypersensitivity, hemolysis, nephrotoxicity, hematologic effects.
Do not confuse: Ceftriaxone vs Ceftazidime vs Cefepime
Ceftriaxone (3rd gen)
  • No Pseudomonas coverage
  • Crosses BBB → meningitis, gonorrhea, CAP
  • Biliary excretion, neonatal jaundice/pseudolithiasis risk
Ceftazidime / Cefepime
  • Ceftazidime (3rd gen) and Cefepime (4th gen) both cover Pseudomonas
  • Cefepime is broader: Gram+, Gram−, AmpC-resistant
  • Neither is a first choice for empirical meningitis the way ceftriaxone is
Fast distinction: If the question mentions Pseudomonas coverage, the answer is ceftazidime or cefepime — never ceftriaxone.
Exam trap
Cephalosporin "generation" number is not a complete predictor of spectrum. Ceftaroline (5th gen) does NOT cover Pseudomonas despite being a "later" generation — its special feature is MRSA coverage, not more Gram-negative reach.
Which cephalosporin generation is the gold standard for surgical prophylaxis, and why?
1st generation (cefazolin) — strong Gram-positive (skin flora) coverage, which is what most surgical site infections come from.
Monobactam (Aztreonam) Page 4 Should Know ▼
Must know
  • Spectrum: aerobic Gram-negative rods only (e.g. Neisseria, Pseudomonas) — zero Gram-positive or anaerobic activity.
  • Mechanism: binds and inhibits PBPs/transpeptidases, just like other beta-lactams, but the unfused monocyclic ring means antibodies don't recognize it the same way.
  • No cross-allergenicity with penicillins/cephalosporins — safe in severe penicillin allergy for Gram-negative infections. Exception: ceftazidime shares an identical side chain → cross-allergy with aztreonam specifically.
Should know
  • Uses: hospital-acquired UTI/biliary/GI/GU infections, cystic fibrosis, pyelonephritis, septicemia, peritonitis, endometritis.
  • Side effects: skin rash, abnormal LFTs, cross-sensitivity with cephalosporin allergy (see exception above), GI upset, abnormal taste.
Exam trap
Aztreonam is the go-to for Gram-negative coverage in a penicillin-allergic patient — unless the allergy is specifically to ceftazidime, in which case aztreonam is cross-reactive too.
Carbapenems Pages 4–5 Must Know ▼
Must know
  • Agents: Imipenem, Meropenem, Doripenem (Group 2) and Ertapenem (Group 1).
  • Imipenem needs cilastatin — imipenem is hydrolyzed by renal dehydropeptidase-1 in the proximal tubule, which both inactivates the drug and produces nephrotoxic metabolites. Cilastatin blocks that enzyme.
  • Meropenem, Doripenem, Ertapenem are structurally modified to resist dehydropeptidase-1 — no cilastatin needed.
  • Ertapenem uniquely LACKS activity against Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, and Enterococcus — but is long-acting (once daily).
  • Imipenem seizure risk: competes with GABA at the receptor → neurotoxicity, worse at high doses and in renal failure. If seizure occurs → discontinue the drug.
Mechanism of action
Penetrates the bacterial cell wall, binds PBPs (transpeptidases)
↓
Highly resistant to most beta-lactamases (including penicillinase-producing staph, some MRSA)
↓
Interferes with cell-wall component synthesis → cell death
Should know
  • Chemistry: very similar to penicillin (penam), but the sulfur at position 1 is replaced with a carbon → unsaturation introduced → hence "carbapenem." Thienamycin (1976) was the first discovered.
  • Uses: nosocomial septicemia, febrile neutropenia, intra-abdominal/pelvic infection, respiratory/ENT/GU infection, multidrug-resistant infections.
  • Side effects: seizures (high dose), GI upset, rash, partial cross-sensitivity with penicillin allergy, headache, pruritus.
  • All carbapenems need renal dose adjustment.
Do not confuse: Imipenem vs Meropenem vs Ertapenem
Imipenem
  • Needs cilastatin (renal dehydropeptidase-1 inhibitor)
  • Highest seizure risk
Meropenem / Ertapenem
  • Meropenem: no cilastatin needed, safe for CNS/meningitis use, covers Pseudomonas
  • Ertapenem: no cilastatin, once-daily, but NO Pseudomonas/Acinetobacter/Enterococcus coverage
Fast distinction: "Needs cilastatin" = imipenem. "Once-daily but weak spectrum" = ertapenem.
Exam trap
Don't assume every carbapenem covers Pseudomonas — ertapenem is the carbapenem exception with no reliable antipseudomonal activity.
Why is imipenem co-administered with cilastatin?
Cilastatin blocks renal dehydropeptidase-1, the enzyme that both inactivates imipenem in the proximal tubule and generates nephrotoxic metabolites.
How Bacteria Evade Beta-Lactams Page 2 Must Know ▼
StrategyWhat happens
Destroy the drugBeta-lactamases (penicillinases, cephalosporinases, carbapenemases) hydrolyze the ring → inactive penicilloic acid
Change the targetLow-affinity PBPs, e.g. PBP2a in MRSA (mecA gene), altered PBPs in resistant S. pneumoniae
Keep the drug outPorin loss/mutation in Gram-negative outer membrane blocks hydrophilic beta-lactams
Pump the drug outActive multidrug efflux pumps clear the drug from the periplasmic space
Mnemonic (from the lecture)Destroy · Change · Keep out · Pump out — the lecturer's own "important to know" list, in that exact order.
What mutation specifically causes MRSA resistance and what does it change?
mecA gene encodes PBP2a, a penicillin-binding protein with very low affinity for beta-lactams — the target itself is changed, not destroyed.

II. Glycopeptides & Related Cell Wall/Membrane Agents

Vancomycin is the workhorse; know its resistance mechanism (D-Ala-D-Lac) and why red man syndrome isn't a true allergy.
Vancomycin Page 5–6 Must Know ▼
Mechanism of action
Binds directly to the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of the peptidoglycan precursor (NOT a PBP)
↓
Forms 5 hydrogen bonds → caps the precursor
↓
Blocks transglycosylase (sugar linking) AND transpeptidase (cross-linking)
↓
Late-stage, extracellular action → bactericidal
Must know
  • Resistance (VRE/VISA): D-Ala-D-Ala → D-Ala-D-Lactate (VanA/VanB) or D-Ala-D-Serine → loses 1 H-bond → 1000-fold drop in binding affinity.
  • IV for systemic MRSA infection (poor oral absorption). Oral only for C. difficile colitis — stays in the gut, not absorbed.
  • TDM mandatory: trough target 15–20 mcg/mL for severe MRSA. ~90% cleared by glomerular filtration.
  • Red Man Syndrome (Vancomycin Infusion Reaction) — NOT a true allergy, non-immunologic direct mast-cell histamine release, rate-dependent. Fix = slow infusion over 1–2h ± antihistamine, don't necessarily stop the drug.
  • Nephrotoxicity (dose-related AKI, very common, worse with prolonged high troughs or concurrent aminoglycosides) and ototoxicity (less common, often irreversible: tinnitus, vertigo, hearing loss).
Should know
  • Half-life ~6 hours. Indications: septicemia, endocarditis, bone infection, skin/soft tissue, pneumonia, MRSA, C. difficile.
  • Drug interactions: additive nephro/ototoxicity with aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, NSAIDs; many others listed in lecture (cefepime, ciprofloxacin, piperacillin-tazobactam, etc.).
  • If trough too low → give the dose again (don't skip). If trough too high → hold/skip a dose, don't just push through.
Do not confuse: IV vancomycin vs Oral vancomycin
IV vancomycin
  • Treats systemic infection (bacteremia, endocarditis, MRSA)
  • Requires TDM (trough 15-20)
  • Poor oral absorption is why it MUST be IV for systemic disease
Oral vancomycin
  • Treats C. difficile colitis ONLY (acts locally in the gut)
  • Not systemically absorbed — does NOT treat bacteremia
  • Never used for anything outside the GI tract
Fast distinction: If the question says "bacteremia" → IV. If it says "C. diff colitis" → oral. Mixing these up is a classic trap.
Exam trap
Red man syndrome mimics an allergic reaction (flushing, rash) but is histamine release, not IgE-mediated. Slowing the infusion (or premedicating) is often enough — you don't have to abandon a needed antibiotic.
What is the genetic basis of vancomycin resistance in VRE?
Substitution of the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala with D-Ala-D-Lactate (VanA/VanB), which removes a critical hydrogen bond and drops vancomycin binding affinity ~1000-fold.
Oritavancin & Teicoplanin (Lipoglycopeptides) Page 6 Should Know ▼
DrugKey points
OritavancinInhibits transglycosylation + transpeptidation. Active against VRSA and VRE. Still being evaluated (Phase IV) for skin/soft tissue and MRSA infections.
TeicoplaninSame MOA as vancomycin (binds D-Ala-D-Ala). Think "vancomycin with a much longer half-life" (~70–100 h, dosed every 3–4 days). Gram-positive only, including MRSA/MRSE. Used for endocarditis, bone/joint infection, C. difficile colitis (oral). Adverse effects mirror vancomycin: rash, fever, nephrotoxicity, rare ototoxicity.
Miscellaneous Cell Wall / Membrane Agents Page 6 Should Know ▼
Table 3.06. Miscellaneous cell wall/membrane agents
DrugMechanismSpectrum / UseKey toxicity
DaptomycinLipopeptide. Binds bacterial plasma membrane → depolarization → ion leakage → cell death (different from vancomycin, which hits the wall precursor)Gram-positive incl. VRE/VRSA. MRSA and VRE skin/soft tissue infection, bacteremiaMyopathy (monitor CPK). Inactivated by pulmonary surfactant — NEVER use for pneumonia
BacitracinInhibits cell-wall synthesisGram-positive (strep, staph, enterococci); highly sensitive: Corynebacterium, gonococci, meningococci, Cl. tetani, Treponema, H. influenzae. Topical only (antiseptic)Marked nephrotoxicity → systemic use abandoned
FosfomycinInhibits an early step of peptidoglycan synthesis (before beta-lactams act)S. aureus, strep, Enterobacteriaceae, H. influenzae, Neisseria. Exam trap
Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant — if the vignette is pneumonia, daptomycin is a wrong answer even though it covers the right organism (MRSA).

III–IX. Protein Synthesis Inhibitors

30S blockers (tetracyclines, aminoglycosides) and 50S blockers (macrolides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, linezolid). Most are bacteriostatic; aminoglycosides are the bactericidal exception.
Overview: Selective Toxicity & the 30S/50S Split Page 7 Must Know ▼
Must know
  • Most protein synthesis inhibitors are bacteriostatic — they don't kill the bacteria directly, they just halt growth so the host immune system can clean up.
  • Exception: aminoglycosides are bactericidal (irreversible 30S binding + membrane damage from misread proteins).
  • Mitochondria have their own 70S-like ribosomes — this is why prolonged/high-dose therapy with some of these drugs (chloramphenicol, linezolid) still causes host toxicity.
Mnemonic (Lecturer's mnemonic)"Buy AT 30, CELL for 50" — Aminoglycosides, Tetracyclines = 30S inhibitors. Chloramphenicol, Erythromycin (macrolides), Linezolid, Lincosamides (clindamycin) = 50S inhibitors.
Table 12 (Comprehensive Reviewer). Antibacterials at a glance — ribosomal targets
TargetDrug classesTypical effect
30S ribosomeAminoglycosides, TetracyclinesAminoglycosides = bactericidal · Tetracyclines = static
50S ribosomeMacrolides, Clindamycin, Chloramphenicol, Linezolid, StreptograminsMostly static, occasionally cidal for select organisms
Do not confuse: 30S drugs vs 50S drugs
30S (early decoding)
  • Tetracyclines: reversibly block the A-site → bacteriostatic
  • Aminoglycosides: irreversibly bind, cause misreading → bactericidal
50S (elongation/initiation)
  • Macrolides & clindamycin: block the exit tunnel/translocation
  • Chloramphenicol: blocks peptidyl transferase directly
  • Linezolid: blocks 70S initiation complex assembly (earliest possible step)
Fast distinction: "Blocks the A-site so aminoacyl-tRNA can't enter" = tetracycline (30S). "Blocks the initiation complex before translation even starts" = linezolid (50S).
Tetracyclines Pages 7–9 Must Know ▼
Tetracycline translation arrest
Drug enters and accumulates in the bacterial cell (passive diffusion + active transport)
↓
Reversibly binds the 30S subunit at the 16S rRNA
↓
Sterically blocks aminoacyl-tRNA from reaching the A-site
↓
No new amino acids added → chain elongation halts → bacteriostatic (reversible on drug withdrawal)
Must know
  • Classification by duration: Short (6–8h: tetracycline, chlortetracycline, oxytetracycline) · Intermediate (12h: demeclocycline, methacycline) · Long (16–18h: doxycycline, minocycline, tigecycline).
  • First choice for: atypical pneumonia, cholera, brucellosis, plague, relapsing fever, Rocky Mountain spotted fever (rickettsia), Chlamydia, Lyme disease. Doxycycline = prophylaxis for leptospirosis.
  • Contraindicated: pregnancy and children <8 years — chelates calcium in developing teeth/bone → permanent discoloration + growth inhibition.
  • Chelates divalent/trivalent cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, Fe2+, Al3+) → do not take with dairy, antacids, or iron — blocks absorption.
  • Resistance: efflux pumps (Tet(A-E) in Gram-neg, Tet(K) in staph) pump the drug out; ribosomal protection proteins (Tet(M)) physically dislodge the drug from the ribosome; enzymatic inactivation (monooxygenase).
  • Tigecycline overcomes both mechanisms — bulky side chain resists efflux pumps and Tet(M) protection — but lacks reliable Pseudomonas/Proteus coverage and gives low serum levels.
Should know
  • Second choice for: tetanus, anthrax, gonorrhea, syphilis, pneumonia, COPD prophylaxis.
  • Doxycycline/minocycline well absorbed orally; tigecycline is IV-only. Doxycycline is eliminated non-renally (feces) — no renal adjustment needed, unlike most others.
  • Additional toxicities: GI upset, esophageal ulcer/odynophagia, hepatic necrosis, Fanconi syndrome, photosensitivity, vestibular effects (minocycline), demeclocycline → nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Exam trap
A patient on doxycycline with severe photosensitivity + esophageal irritation from swallowing the pill without water and lying down right after — both are classic tetracycline exam pearls (take with water, remain upright).
Why must tetracyclines be avoided in young children and pregnancy?
They chelate calcium and bind to developing bone and teeth, causing permanent tooth discoloration and inhibited bone growth.
Macrolides & Ketolides Pages 9–10 Must Know ▼
Mechanism of action
Reversibly binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit
↓
Blocks translocation of peptidyl-tRNA from the A-site to the P-site (obstructs the exit tunnel)
↓
Chain elongation halts → bacteriostatic
Must know
  • Erythromycin is acid-labile → needs enteric coating/stable salts. Clarithromycin & azithromycin are acid-stable, better absorbed.
  • Azithromycin: massive volume of distribution, 68-hour half-life → short 3-day courses possible. Lacks the 14-membered ring → no CYP3A4 inhibition, fewer drug interactions.
  • Erythromycin & clarithromycin are potent CYP3A4 inhibitors → raise levels of statins, warfarin, theophylline.
  • QTc prolongation → Torsades de Pointes risk (blocks cardiac hERG K+ channels), worse with fluoroquinolones or antiarrhythmics on board.
  • Ketolides (telithromycin): bind 2 sites on the 50S subunit for higher potency against resistant strains, but severe hepatotoxicity restricts use to CAP only.
Should know
  • Erythromycin stimulates motilin receptors → GI upset (also used off-label as a prokinetic). Erythromycin estolate → cholestatic jaundice.
  • Resistance: 23S rRNA methylation (erm gene), efflux (mef), enzymatic inactivation.
Do not confuse: Azithromycin vs Erythromycin/Clarithromycin
Azithromycin
  • No CYP3A4 inhibition → fewer interactions
  • Very long half-life → short course (3 days)
  • "Safer" macrolide for statin/warfarin patients
Erythromycin / Clarithromycin
  • Potent CYP3A4 inhibitors → statin/warfarin/theophylline toxicity risk
  • Erythromycin is acid-labile, needs special formulation
  • Both still carry QTc prolongation risk
Fast distinction: If a question pairs a macrolide with statin-induced rhabdomyolysis, the drug is clarithromycin or erythromycin, not azithromycin.
Exam trap
Don't assume all macrolides are interchangeable — azithromycin's whole clinical advantage is the absence of CYP3A4 inhibition, which the exam loves to test with a "safer macrolide for this interacting drug" question.
Which macrolide is preferred in a patient already on warfarin or a statin, and why?
Azithromycin — it lacks the 14-membered ring responsible for CYP3A4 inhibition, so it does not raise warfarin or statin levels the way erythromycin/clarithromycin do.
Clindamycin Pages 9–10 Must Know ▼
Must know
  • Best-in-class anaerobic coverage above the diaphragm: aspiration pneumonia, lung abscess, deep oral infections. Excellent bone/joint penetration (osteomyelitis) but does NOT cross the BBB.
  • Antitoxin effect: shuts down ribosomal synthesis of bacterial exotoxins and M-protein → used as an adjunct in necrotizing fasciitis / toxic shock syndrome (strep or staph) to stop the cytokine storm.
  • Black box: pseudomembranous colitis (C. difficile) — wipes out protective gut flora, allowing C. diff overgrowth, exotoxin release, pseudomembrane formation. Clindamycin is one of the highest-risk antibiotics for this.
Should know
  • Reserve for serious infections where alternatives aren't appropriate — avoid for viral/minor infections.
  • D-test: an isolate that looks erythromycin-resistant but clindamycin-susceptible may actually have inducible clindamycin resistance — needs the D-test to unmask it.
Do not confuse: Clindamycin's two very different clinical uses
Anaerobic / antitoxin
  • Aspiration pneumonia, lung abscess
  • Necrotizing fasciitis (blocks toxin production)
  • Excellent bone/joint penetration
Its own worst side effect
  • Kills protective gut flora
  • Highest-risk drug (with fluoroquinolones, broad-spectrum beta-lactams) for C. difficile colitis
  • Black box warning
Fast distinction: Clindamycin is simultaneously one of the best anti-toxin drugs and one of the biggest C. diff risks — the exam tests both sides.
Exam trap
Clindamycin is added to a beta-lactam in severe strep/staph infections specifically to suppress toxin production, not because it's a stronger cell-killer — the beta-lactam does the killing, clindamycin quiets the toxin.
Why is clindamycin combined with a beta-lactam in necrotizing fasciitis?
Clindamycin suppresses ribosomal synthesis of streptococcal/staphylococcal exotoxins (antitoxin effect), which the beta-lactam alone does not do, while the beta-lactam provides bactericidal killing.
Chloramphenicol Pages 10–11 Must Know ▼
Mechanism of action
Binds the 50S subunit near the acceptor site
↓
Directly inhibits peptidyl transferase
↓
Prevents peptide bond formation → translation freezes → usually bacteriostatic (bactericidal against H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae)
Must know
  • Three distinct toxicities to keep separate:
Chloramphenicol's three signature toxicities
ToxicityMechanismKey feature
Bone marrow suppressionReversible inhibition of host mitochondrial (70S-like) ribosomesDose-dependent, reversible on stopping the drug
Aplastic anemiaIdiosyncratic, nitroso reactive intermediates damage DNADose-INDEPENDENT, rare, often fatal, can appear weeks-months later
Gray baby syndromeNeonates lack UDP-glucuronyl transferase → can't conjugate the drug → toxic accumulationCirculatory collapse: gray skin, blue lips, limp tone, high mortality
Must know
  • Crosses the placenta and is secreted in breast milk — relevant to gray baby syndrome risk.
  • Excellent CSF penetration — historically used for bacterial meningitis and typhoid, now reserved for life-threatening MDR pathogens (e.g. VRE) or severe rickettsial disease when nothing else works.
Should know
  • Resistance: R-plasmid acetyltransferase inactivates the drug, altered 50S affinity, decreased penetration.
  • Still widely used in veterinary medicine (much lower toxicity in animals).
Do not confuse: Reversible marrow suppression vs Aplastic anemia (both chloramphenicol)
Reversible suppression
  • Dose-dependent
  • Resolves after stopping the drug
  • Anemia/leukopenia/thrombocytopenia
Aplastic anemia
  • Idiosyncratic, NOT dose-related
  • Can be permanent/fatal
  • Can appear long after therapy stops, may progress to leukemia
Fast distinction: "Dose-related and reversible" = marrow suppression. "Rare, unpredictable, and potentially fatal" = aplastic anemia. These are two separate mechanisms, not two severities of the same thing.
Exam trap
Gray baby syndrome happens because neonates lack UDP-glucuronyl transferase, NOT because of a direct "immature kidney" excretion problem — the defect is in hepatic conjugation.
What enzyme deficiency in neonates causes gray baby syndrome?
Immature/absent UDP-glucuronyl transferase, so chloramphenicol cannot be conjugated and accumulates to toxic levels.
Linezolid (Zyvox) Pages 10, 25 Must Know ▼
Mechanism of action
Binds a specific pocket on the 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit
↓
Prevents assembly of the 70S initiation complex (30S + 50S + fMet-tRNA can't join)
↓
Translation never starts — earliest possible block point → bacteriostatic
Must know
  • 100% oral bioavailability → seamless IV-to-PO switch, a major practical advantage over IV vancomycin.
  • Thrombocytopenia in up to 30% of patients, especially past 2 weeks of therapy → monitor CBC/platelets.
  • Reversible, non-selective MAO inhibitor → risk of serotonin syndrome with SSRIs/other serotonergic drugs, and a weak tyramine reaction risk with tyramine-rich foods.
  • Long-term use: peripheral and optic neuropathy (can be irreversible), lactic acidosis.
Should know
  • Indications: nosocomial/CAP pneumonia, skin/soft tissue infection, resistant Gram-positive infection, VRE bacteremia.
  • Dosing: 600mg IV/PO q12h, typically 10–14 days — but limit duration when possible because of hematologic/neurologic toxicity.
Do not confuse: Linezolid vs Daptomycin vs Vancomycin (all cover resistant Gram-positives)
Linezolid
  • Covers MRSA pneumonia (unlike daptomycin)
  • 100% oral bioavailability
  • Risk: thrombocytopenia, serotonin syndrome
Daptomycin
  • Does NOT cover pneumonia (surfactant inactivates it)
  • Rapidly bactericidal
  • Risk: myopathy/CPK elevation
Fast distinction: "Works in pneumonia" → linezolid or vancomycin, not daptomycin. "On an SSRI" → be careful with linezolid (serotonin syndrome).
Exam trap
Linezolid + an SSRI/SNRI/MAOI is a classic drug-interaction question — the mechanism is linezolid's own MAO-inhibiting activity stacking with serotonergic drugs.
Why does linezolid cover pneumonia but daptomycin does not?
Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant, so it cannot be used for pneumonia; linezolid has no such limitation and achieves good lung tissue penetration.
Aminoglycosides & Spectinomycin Pages 11–15 Must Know ▼
Must know
  • Uptake needs oxygen: passive diffusion through Gram-negative porins into periplasm (Phase 1) → then energy/oxygen-dependent active transport across the inner membrane via the proton motive force (Phase 2/3). This is why aminoglycosides are useless against anaerobes.
  • Once inside: irreversibly binds the 30S subunit → misreads mRNA codons → defective/aberrant proteins get inserted into the cell membrane → membrane damage → leakage → bactericidal (irreversible binding + membrane damage, unlike the reversible/static tetracyclines).
  • Concentration-dependent killing (higher Cmax/MIC = more killing) + long post-antibiotic effect (PAE, 2–6h) → supports once-daily (extended-interval) dosing: one large dose (5–7 mg/kg) → high peak → 18–24h washout window with trough <1 mcg/mL.
  • Synergy with cell-wall-active agents (penicillin, vancomycin): the beta-lactam weakens the wall, letting more aminoglycoside in → gold standard for enterococcal/staphylococcal endocarditis (gentamicin + ampicillin/vancomycin).
  • Toxicity triad: Nephrotoxicity (reversible AKI, proximal tubule accumulation, earliest sign = rising trough level, not creatinine), Ototoxicity (irreversible; cochlear = amikacin/tobramycin/kanamycin, vestibular = streptomycin/gentamicin; worsened by loop diuretics), Neuromuscular blockade (blocks presynaptic Ca2+ channels → treat with calcium gluconate then neostigmine; contraindicated in myasthenia gravis).
Should know
  • Once-daily dosing avoided if CrCl <60 mL/min — use traditional divided dosing instead.
  • Poor dialysis clearance (only 40–60% for gentamicin via hemodialysis).
  • Resistance: enzymatic modification (acetylation/AAC, phosphorylation/APH, adenylylation/ANT — most clinically important mechanism), decreased penetration (porin/PMF loss), ribosomal target alteration.
  • Amikacin & Plazomicin resist most modifying enzymes — amikacin is a key second-line MDR-TB agent; plazomicin targets CRE (carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae), needs trough-only monitoring (<3 mcg/mL).
  • Tobramycin: slightly better than gentamicin against Pseudomonas; inhaled formulation for cystic fibrosis (28 days on/28 days off) minimizes systemic toxicity.
  • Spectinomycin: aminocyclitol (structurally related but NOT a true aminoglycoside — lacks amino sugars/glycosidic bonds), binds 30S reversibly → bacteriostatic (not bactericidal). Used almost exclusively for drug-resistant gonorrhea; poor efficacy for pharyngeal gonorrhea.
Do not confuse: Gentamicin vs Tobramycin vs Amikacin
Gentamicin
  • Classic synergy partner for enterococcal/staph endocarditis
  • Higher vestibulotoxicity risk
Tobramycin / Amikacin
  • Tobramycin: preferred for Pseudomonas, inhaled CF formulation
  • Amikacin: resists most modifying enzymes — used when gentamicin/tobramycin fail, key MDR-TB agent
Fast distinction: "Resistant to Gentamicin AND Tobramycin, still susceptible" → the answer is amikacin.
Exam trap
Aminoglycosides should never be used as monotherapy for pneumonia — acidic, low-oxygen infected lung tissue impairs the active-transport uptake step, and pulmonary penetration is poor.
Why are aminoglycosides ineffective against anaerobes?
Their uptake into the bacterial cytoplasm requires active, oxygen-dependent transport driven by the proton motive force — anaerobes cannot generate this, so the drug never reaches the ribosome.

X–XI. Antimetabolites & Antifolate Drugs

Sulfonamides and trimethoprim both exploit the fact that bacteria must build their own folate from scratch, while mammals simply absorb it from the diet.
Why Antifolates Are Selectively Toxic Pages 15–16 Must Know ▼
Must know
  • Mammals completely lack de novo folate synthesis enzymes — they absorb preformed dietary folic acid via specialized transporters.
  • Bacteria cannot import folate at all — they are impermeable to it — and must synthesize tetrahydrofolic acid (THF) from scratch, starting with PABA.
  • THF is the essential carbon-donor coenzyme for making purines, thymidine, and methionine — the building blocks of DNA/RNA/protein.
  • Block the bacterial folate pathway → block DNA production → selective toxicity, because human cells never needed that pathway in the first place.
Sulfonamides Pages 15–18 Must Know ▼
Mechanism of action
Sulfonamide structurally resembles PABA (para-aminobenzenesulfonamide core)
↓
Competitively, reversibly binds dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS) active site
↓
Blocks dihydropteroic acid formation (or gets incorporated as a dead-end false substrate)
↓
Folate synthesis halts → bacteriostatic (halts division, doesn't kill existing cells)
Must know
  • Classification by duration: Short (sulfadiazine, 4–8h) · Intermediate (sulfamethoxazole, 8–12h) · Long (sulfadoxine, 7 days) · Other (mafenide, sulfacetamide).
  • Weak acids → low solubility in acidic urine (pH <5.5) → crystalluria risk — prevent with hydration + urine alkalinization.
  • Stevens-Johnson Syndrome / TEN — sulfonamides are classic triggers.
  • G6PD deficiency → hemolytic anemia (oxidative stress on RBCs).
  • Displaces bilirubin from albumin → kernicterus risk if given late in pregnancy/near term — contraindicated then.
Should know
  • Resistance: altered DHPS affinity, PABA hyperproduction (up to 70-fold, outcompetes the drug), decreased accumulation (porin/efflux changes).
  • Topical/specialty uses: sulfacetamide (ophthalmic, conjunctivitis), silver sulfadiazine/mafenide (burn wounds), sulfasalazine (splits into sulfapyridine + 5-ASA for ulcerative colitis).
  • Also cause: nausea, epigastric pain, photosensitivity, hepatitis, hemolysis.
What natural substrate does a sulfonamide structurally mimic, and what enzyme does it block?
PABA (p-aminobenzoic acid); it competitively blocks dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS).
Trimethoprim Pages 17–18 Must Know ▼
Mechanism of action
Structurally mimics the pteridine portion of folic acid
↓
Reversibly, competitively binds dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR)
↓
Blocks conversion of dihydrofolate → tetrahydrofolate (THF)
↓
One-carbon donors depleted → nucleotide synthesis halts → bacteriostatic
Must know
  • Bacterial DHFR is 10,000–100,000× more sensitive to trimethoprim than mammalian DHFR — this huge selectivity gap is what makes it safe.
  • Weak base → ion trapping in acidic fluids (urine, prostatic fluid, vaginal secretions) → very high local concentrations → excellent for prostatitis/UTI/vaginitis.
  • 60–80% excreted unchanged in urine. Half-life 10–12h, closely matched to sulfamethoxazole's ~10h — this is deliberate, it's what allows a stable combination ratio.
  • Pyrimethamine is a related DHFR inhibitor, but selective for protozoal DHFR — used for malaria/toxoplasmosis, not typically as an antibacterial.
Should know
  • Toxicity: megaloblastic anemia/leukopenia/thrombocytopenia from folate blockade (reversed by folinic acid/leucovorin, which bacteria cannot use). Acts as a weak potassium-sparing diuretic → hyperkalemia.
Why does folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue a patient from trimethoprim-induced marrow suppression without rescuing the bacteria?
Human cells can take up and use folinic acid directly (bypassing the DHFR block), but bacteria have no folate transport system and cannot import it — so only the host is rescued.
Sequential Blockade: TMP-SMX Pages 17–18, 25 Must Know ▼
Must know
  • Sulfamethoxazole blocks the early step (DHPS), trimethoprim blocks the late step (DHFR) — same pathway, two sequential enzymes.
  • Individually both are bacteriostatic. Combined in a 5:1 ratio (TMP:SMX), the blockade is so complete it becomes bactericidal against susceptible strains.
  • Resistance develops much more slowly for the combination than for either drug alone — a bacterium needs simultaneous mutations in both DHPS AND DHFR to survive.
Must know
  • Drug of choice for: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) prophylaxis + treatment in HIV/immunocompromised, and Nocardia infections.
  • Also used for: uncomplicated UTI, community-associated MRSA skin infection (backup), Listeria (penicillin-allergic alternative). Sulfadiazine + pyrimethamine (not TMP) is the regimen for toxoplasmosis.
Should know
  • 50–80% of AIDS patients on TMP-SMX develop severe hypersensitivity reactions (fever, rash, leukopenia, diarrhea) — a well-known exam association.
  • Resistance principles overall: change the target, overwhelm the inhibitor (PABA/DHFR overproduction), or reduce intracellular drug (porins/efflux).
Do not confuse: Sulfamethoxazole alone vs Trimethoprim alone vs TMP-SMX
Either drug ALONE
  • Bacteriostatic only
  • Growth inhibited, not killed
  • Resistance can develop faster to a single agent
TMP-SMX COMBINED
  • Sequential double-strike on 2 enzymes
  • Complete folate depletion → bactericidal
  • Resistance evolves much more slowly (needs 2 simultaneous mutations)
Fast distinction: "Sequential blockade" and "why is TMP-SMX bactericidal when each drug alone is bacteriostatic" are the two most common ways this concept is tested.
Exam trap
TMP-SMX in an AIDS/HIV patient carries a very high (50-80%) rate of hypersensitivity reaction — a common exam vignette is a PJP-prophylaxis patient developing fever and rash on TMP-SMX.
Why is TMP-SMX bactericidal when each component alone is bacteriostatic?
Sulfamethoxazole blocks DHPS (early folate synthesis) while trimethoprim blocks DHFR (late folate synthesis) in the same pathway — blocking both sequential steps together causes complete folate depletion, which kills the bacteria rather than just halting growth.

XII. Fluoroquinolones

DNA gyrase and Topoisomerase IV inhibitors. Rapidly bactericidal, but the toxicity profile (tendons, cartilage, aorta, QTc) is why current guidelines say "use restraint."
Fluoroquinolones: Overview & Generations Pages 18–20 Must Know ▼
Table 9. Fluoroquinolone generations
GenerationAgentsSpectrum focusKey clinical use
1stNalidixic acid, NorfloxacinGram-negative aerobic bacilli onlyUncomplicated UTI only
2ndCiprofloxacin, OfloxacinExpanded Gram-neg incl. Pseudomonas; some atypicalsComplicated UTI, prostatitis, infectious diarrhea, anthrax prophylaxis
3rdLevofloxacin, Gemifloxacin, MoxifloxacinEnhanced Gram-positive (S. pneumoniae) + atypicalsRespiratory fluoroquinolones — CAP, atypical pneumonia
AdvancedMoxifloxacin, DelafloxacinAdds anaerobes (Bacteroides); delafloxacin adds MRSAIntra-abdominal, pelvic, complicated skin infection
Must know
  • Only Ciprofloxacin and Levofloxacin are reliably antipseudomonal among the commonly used agents.
  • Moxifloxacin is the outlier: adds anaerobic coverage but is NOT reliably antipseudomonal and is NOT used for UTI (see PK section below).
Fluoroquinolone Mechanism of Action Pages 18–19 Must Know ▼
Dual-targeting mechanism
Inhibits DNA gyrase (Topoisomerase II) — primary target in Gram-negative bacteria — normally relieves positive supercoiling ahead of the replication fork
↓
Inhibits Topoisomerase IV — primary target in Gram-positive bacteria — normally separates (decatenates) daughter chromosomes after replication
↓
Traps the enzyme-DNA cleavable complex mid-cut → lethal double-strand DNA breaks
↓
Genomic fragmentation → rapidly bactericidal, concentration-dependent with a post-antibiotic effect
Must know
  • Dual-target strategy means high-level resistance needs mutations in BOTH enzymes simultaneously — much rarer than single-target resistance.
Fluoroquinolone Pharmacokinetics Page 19 Must Know ▼
Must know
  • 70–95% oral bioavailability → easy IV-to-PO switch.
  • Cation chelation: the quinolone carboxylic acid group binds Mg2+, Al3+, Ca2+, Fe2+ → forms insoluble complexes → blocks absorption. Avoid antacids, calcium, iron/sucralfate, dairy — separate dosing by 2–6 hours.
  • Most agents (cipro, levo, ofloxacin) are renally cleared — probenecid blocks tubular secretion → raises serum levels. Dose reduction needed if CrCl <50 mL/min.
  • Moxifloxacin is the exception: hepatic metabolism + biliary excretion → no renal adjustment needed, BUT does not reach therapeutic urine levels → never use moxifloxacin for a UTI.
Fluoroquinolone Resistance Pages 19–20 Should Know ▼
Must know
  • QRDR mutations: gyrA (Gram-negatives) or parC (Gram-positives) → 10–100-fold lower drug binding.
  • Historical example: rapid gyrA mutation in Neisseria gonorrhoeae in the 1990s made ciprofloxacin obsolete for gonorrhea — ceftriaxone is now standard of care.
Should know
  • Efflux pumps (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, M. tuberculosis) and porin loss (Pseudomonas, Serratia — OprD) also contribute.
  • Plasmid-mediated Qnr proteins protect DNA gyrase → adds another layer, can stack with other mechanisms for high-level resistance.
Fluoroquinolone Toxicity Page 20 Must Know ▼
Must know
  • Tendinitis/Achilles tendon rupture — magnesium chelation disrupts collagen; risk highest in elderly, renal failure, concurrent corticosteroids.
  • Cartilage damage (arthropathy) — contraindicated in children <18 and pregnancy unless no alternative exists (e.g. anthrax, CF).
  • Aortic aneurysm/dissection risk — collagen disruption extends to the vessel wall.
  • QTc prolongation (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — avoid with Class IA/III antiarrhythmics.
  • CNS toxicity — GABA receptor inhibition → headache, dizziness, insomnia, seizures.
  • Dysglycemia (hypo- or hyperglycemia) — gatifloxacin was withdrawn for this.
  • Phototoxicity — UVA-triggered sunburn-like reactions.
Exam trap
A pregnant patient, a child under 18, or someone already on an antiarrhythmic/with a prolonged QTc are all reasons to actively AVOID fluoroquinolones, not just "use with caution" — current stewardship guidance reserves them for infections with no safer alternative.
Name the 4 organ systems most associated with fluoroquinolone black-box warnings.
Tendons (rupture), cartilage (arthropathy, pediatric/pregnancy), the aorta (aneurysm/dissection), and the heart (QTc prolongation) — plus CNS and glucose effects.
Systemic Drug Summary: TMP-SMX & the Fluoroquinolones Page 36 Should Know ▼
Do not confuse: Ciprofloxacin vs Levofloxacin vs Moxifloxacin
Ciprofloxacin
  • Strongest classic Pseudomonas activity
  • Weaker against S. pneumoniae
  • Complicated UTI, GI infection, bone/joint, anthrax
Levofloxacin / Moxifloxacin
  • Levofloxacin: respiratory + still antipseudomonal, once daily
  • Moxifloxacin: best anaerobic coverage but NOT reliably antipseudomonal, NOT for UTI (hepatic clearance)
Fast distinction: "Respiratory fluoroquinolone that still covers Pseudomonas" = levofloxacin. "Respiratory fluoroquinolone with anaerobic coverage but useless for UTI" = moxifloxacin.

XIII. Common & Serious Adverse Effects, Resistance

Hypersensitivity vs organ toxicity vs superinfection are three DIFFERENT reaction types (Type A vs Type B) — know which bucket each toxicity belongs in.
Hypersensitivity Reactions Page 21 Must Know ▼
Figure 31. Gell & Coombs hypersensitivity types
TypeOnsetManifestationsClassic antibiotics
I (Immediate)Minutes–1 hourUrticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, anaphylaxisPenicillins, cephalosporins
II (Cytotoxic)Hours–daysHemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropeniaPenicillins, cephalosporins, sulfonamides
III (Immune complex)1–3 weeksSerum sickness-like reaction, fever, arthralgia, vasculitisPenicillins, sulfonamides
IV (Delayed)Days–weeksMaculopapular rash, SJS, TEN, contact dermatitisSulfonamides, penicillins, fluoroquinolones
Must know
  • Management sequence: stop the drug → for anaphylaxis, stabilize ABCs and give epinephrine (± IV fluids) → antihistamines/corticosteroids for milder cutaneous symptoms → document the allergy clearly → identify safe alternatives (watch for cross-reactions) → consider supervised desensitization only if the drug is truly irreplaceable.
Exam trap
Not every rash after a penicillin/aminopenicillin is anaphylaxis or even a true allergy (e.g. the ampicillin+EBV rash) — clarify timing, morphology, and severity before labeling a lifelong "penicillin allergy," since over-labeling drives patients toward broader, more toxic alternatives.
Organ-Specific Toxicities Pages 21–22 Must Know ▼
Figure 32 (recreated). Relative toxicity risk by organ system — darker = higher risk
Drug classKidneyLiverCochlea/VestibularCNSBone marrow
Aminoglycosides
Vancomycin
Fluoroquinolones
Macrolides
Anti-TB drugs
Must know
  • Nephrotoxicity: aminoglycosides → acute tubular necrosis; vancomycin → dose-related. Shared risk factors: age >65, baseline CKD, volume depletion, concurrent nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, contrast), therapy >7 days. TDM with individualized dosing cuts risk 40–60%. Trough level (not creatinine) is the earliest warning sign.
  • Ototoxicity: cochlear (amikacin, tobramycin) vs vestibular (gentamicin). Often irreversible, worse with renal impairment or concurrent loop diuretics.
  • Hepatotoxicity: macrolides → cholestatic hepatitis; TMP-SMX → mixed hepatocellular/cholestatic; anti-TB drugs (isoniazid, pyrazinamide) are especially notorious.
  • Neurotoxicity: fluoroquinolones (seizures, psychosis, confusion) and high-dose beta-lactams (Pen G, cefepime, imipenem — seizures, myoclonus, encephalopathy), worse with renal dysfunction/elderly/seizure history.
  • Hematologic: chloramphenicol → aplastic anemia · linezolid → thrombocytopenia · sulfonamides → hemolysis (G6PD deficiency).
Superinfection Pages 21–22 Should Know ▼
Must know
  • Clostridioides difficile colitis is the most clinically significant antibiotic superinfection. Highest-risk agents: fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, broad-spectrum beta-lactams.
  • Risk factors: prolonged course (>7 days), broad-spectrum agents, immunosuppression, ICU admission, indwelling devices, extremes of age, prior antibiotic exposure within 90 days.
Should know
  • Fungal superinfection (oral/vaginal candidiasis) with fluoroquinolones, carbapenems, extended-spectrum penicillins — prevent with antifungal prophylaxis in high-risk patients.
  • Bacterial superinfection: MRSA, VRE, ESBL/CRE Gram-negatives — prevention relies on stewardship and timely de-escalation.
Clinically Significant Drug-Drug Interactions Page 22 Should Know ▼
Rifampin — CYP450 inducer
↓ Warfarin (↓ INR) · ↓ Oral contraceptives (pregnancy risk) · ↓ Protease inhibitors (HIV failure) · ↓ Immunosuppressants (rejection risk) → increases drug metabolism broadly
QT Prolongation
Macrolides + Fluoroquinolones + antiarrhythmics/methadone → ↑ QTc → arrhythmia. Risk amplified by hypokalemia and existing heart disease
Warfarin Interactions
TMP-SMX + warfarin → ↑ INR, ↑ bleeding · Macrolides + warfarin → ↑ INR · Metronidazole + warfarin → ↑ INR — monitor INR, may need to ↓ warfarin dose
Statins + Macrolides
Clarithromycin/Erythromycin ↑ statin levels → myopathy → rhabdomyolysis. Azithromycin is the safer macrolide choice — hold or switch the statin if needed
Exam trap
If a patient on warfarin is started on TMP-SMX, a macrolide, or metronidazole, expect the INR to rise — this is one of the highest-yield DDI patterns across antibiotic exams.
Antimicrobial Resistance & Stewardship Pages 22, 27 Must Know ▼
Table 18. Resistance mechanisms
MechanismExampleResponse
Drug destruction/modificationBeta-lactamases, aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, chloramphenicol acetyltransferaseUse a stable agent or validated inhibitor combination
Altered targetmecA/PBP2a (MRSA), altered PBPs, ribosomal methylation, gyrA/parC changesSelect a different active drug class
Reduced permeabilityGram-negative porin lossCan combine with efflux/enzymes for high-level resistance
EffluxTetracycline, macrolide, fluoroquinolone pumpsRaises the exposure needed; cross-resistance possible
Pathway bypass/overproductionAltered folate enzymes, excess PABAWeakens antimetabolite action
Biofilm/persistersDevices, prostheses, chronic infectionNeeds source control + prolonged/targeted therapy
Must know
  • Genetic routes: spontaneous mutation + selection pressure, OR horizontal gene transfer (conjugation via plasmids, transformation via free DNA, transduction via phages). Transposons/integrons can cluster multiple resistance genes together.
Should know
  • Stewardship checklist ("7 rights"): right indication · right sampling (culture before starting, when safe) · right drug (guideline/antibiogram-informed) · right dose (PK/PD-optimized, organ-adjusted) · right route (IV→PO switch when stable) · right duration (shortest effective course) · right review (antibiotic timeout at 48–72h).
Mnemonic (from the lecture, generalized)Destroy the drug · Change the target · Keep the drug out · Pump the drug out — this same 4-strategy framework (introduced for beta-lactams) applies broadly across almost every resistance mechanism in this lecture.
Special Populations Page 22 Should Know ▼
PopulationAvoidWhy
Pregnancy (all trimesters, safe options)—Penicillins and most cephalosporins are the safe backbone across all trimesters
Pregnancy — avoidTetracyclinesPermanent tooth discoloration, bone growth inhibition
Pregnancy — avoidFluoroquinolonesCartilage toxicity (animal data)
Pregnancy — avoidAminoglycosidesFetal ototoxicity (except for severe infections where benefit outweighs risk)
Pediatric <8 yearsTetracyclinesEnamel hypoplasia, permanent discoloration
Pediatric <18 yearsFluoroquinolonesArthropathy (reserved for serious infection, no alternative)
NeonatesSulfonamidesKernicterus from bilirubin displacement
NeonatesChloramphenicolGray baby syndrome (obsolete in current US practice)

Condensed master tables pulled from the lecture's own comprehensive reviewer section — use these for rapid-fire self-testing in the final 24 hours.

MIC/MBC and PK/PD Patterns Pages 23, 27 (Comprehensive Reviewer) Should Know ▼
MeasureDefinitionInterpretation

MBCLowest concentration killing ~99.9% of the inoculumMBC:MIC ratio may suggest tolerance, not routinely required

Exam trap
A lower MIC does NOT automatically mean a drug is clinically superior — compare the MIC to that specific drug's own breakpoint, achievable tissue exposure, and dosing regimen.
Table 17
PK/PD patternTypical classesDosing implication
Time-dependent (%fT>MIC)Beta-lactamsKeep free concentration above MIC — shorter intervals or prolonged/continuous infusion in severe infection
Concentration-dependent (Cmax/MIC)AminoglycosidesHigher peak relative to MIC = better killing; extended-interval dosing uses the PAE and may reduce toxicity
Exposure-dependent (fAUC/MIC)Vancomycin, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, tetracyclinesOptimize total 24h exposure while respecting toxicity; vancomycin monitoring now focuses on AUC over trough alone

Classic "No Coverage" Reminders Page 27 (Comprehensive Reviewer) Must Know ▼
Must know
  • Aminoglycosides = no anaerobes.
  • Aztreonam = no Gram-positive organisms or anaerobes.
  • Vancomycin / daptomycin / linezolid = no Gram-negative organisms.
  • Daptomycin = no pneumonia (inactivated by pulmonary surfactant).
  • Ertapenem = no reliable Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, or Enterococcus.
  • Ceftriaxone / ceftaroline / moxifloxacin = no reliable Pseudomonas.
  • Nitrofurantoin / fosfomycin = not for pyelonephritis or bacteremia (inadequate tissue/serum levels).
  • Metronidazole = anaerobes/protozoa only, not aerobes.

Commonly Confused Concepts

Cross-class comparisons that don't fit neatly inside a single drug-class card. (Within-class confusions are inside their topic cards above — use search to find more.)
Do not confuse: Beta-lactams vs Vancomycin (both "cell wall," different target)
Beta-lactams
  • Bind PBPs (transpeptidase enzymes)
  • Block cross-linking by inactivating the enzyme
  • Resistance = altered PBP (e.g. PBP2a/MRSA) or beta-lactamase
Vancomycin
  • Binds the D-Ala-D-Ala substrate itself, not an enzyme
  • Blocks both transglycosylation and transpeptidation by capping the precursor
  • Resistance = altered substrate (D-Ala-D-Lac), not an altered enzyme
Fast distinction: "Binds an enzyme" = beta-lactam. "Binds the substrate directly" = vancomycin. This distinction is exactly why MRSA (altered enzyme) is not automatically vancomycin-resistant, and VRE (altered substrate) is not automatically beta-lactam-susceptible.
Do not confuse: Aminoglycosides vs Fluoroquinolones (both concentration-dependent, both bactericidal)
Aminoglycosides
  • Target: 30S ribosome
  • Need oxygen-dependent active transport to enter → no anaerobic activity
  • Toxicity: nephro + oto + neuromuscular blockade
Fluoroquinolones
  • Target: DNA gyrase / Topoisomerase IV
  • Good oral bioavailability, chelated by cations
  • Toxicity: tendons, cartilage, QTc, CNS
Fast distinction: Both show Cmax/MIC-driven killing and a post-antibiotic effect, but they attack completely different machinery (ribosome vs DNA-replication enzymes) and have non-overlapping toxicity profiles.
Do not confuse: Macrolides vs Clindamycin vs Chloramphenicol (all bind 50S, different sub-mechanism)
Macrolides & Clindamycin
  • Bind near the peptidyl transferase center
  • Block translocation (exit tunnel obstruction)
  • Share an overlapping binding site → cross-resistance possible (erm gene, MLS_B)
Chloramphenicol
  • Binds peptidyl transferase directly
  • Blocks peptide BOND FORMATION itself, not just translocation
  • Different resistance gene (acetyltransferase) — no cross-resistance with macrolides
Fast distinction: If the vignette mentions cross-resistance between erythromycin and clindamycin (D-test), that's the macrolide/lincosamide shared site. Chloramphenicol resistance is a separate mechanism entirely.
Do not confuse: Type I vs Type IV Hypersensitivity (antibiotic allergy)
Type I (Immediate)
  • Minutes to 1 hour
  • IgE-mediated
  • Urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, anaphylaxis
  • Classic culprits: penicillins, cephalosporins
Type IV (Delayed)
  • Days to weeks
  • T-cell mediated, non-IgE
  • Maculopapular rash, SJS, TEN, contact dermatitis
  • Classic culprits: sulfonamides, penicillins, fluoroquinolones
Fast distinction: "Anaphylaxis within an hour of the dose" = Type I. "Blistering skin rash appearing a week into therapy" = Type IV (SJS/TEN) — very different urgency and management.
Do not confuse: Reversible toxicity vs Irreversible toxicity (aminoglycosides/vancomycin)
Usually reversible
  • Nephrotoxicity (aminoglycosides, vancomycin) — improves after stopping the drug
  • Neuromuscular blockade — reversible with calcium gluconate/neostigmine
Usually irreversible
  • Ototoxicity (aminoglycosides, vancomycin) — cochlear/vestibular hair cell death does not regenerate
  • Optic/peripheral neuropathy (linezolid, prolonged use)
Fast distinction: "Rising trough, improves after holding the dose" = nephrotoxicity (reversible). "Persistent tinnitus/vertigo after the drug is long gone" = ototoxicity (irreversible).
Do not confuse: Sequential blockade (TMP-SMX) vs Dual-target inhibition (Fluoroquinolones)
TMP-SMX
  • Two DIFFERENT drugs, one pathway (folate synthesis)
  • Each drug alone is bacteriostatic; together = bactericidal
  • Resistance needs mutation in 2 separate ENZYMES for 2 separate DRUGS
Fluoroquinolones
  • ONE drug, two DIFFERENT targets (DNA gyrase + Topo IV)
  • Bactericidal even as monotherapy
  • High-level resistance needs mutation in both targets for the SAME drug
Fast distinction: Both are "hit two targets to slow resistance" strategies, but TMP-SMX achieves it by combining two drugs, while fluoroquinolones achieve it with the dual-binding property of a single molecule.

Exam Traps

Exceptions, opposite effects, and easily-reversed cause-and-effect relationships that are likely to appear as distractors.
Exam trap
Aztreonam is safe in penicillin allergy except if the allergy is to ceftazidime specifically — they share an identical side chain.
Exam trap
Ceftaroline is a "5th generation" cephalosporin but does not cover Pseudomonas — its special feature is MRSA, not more Gram-negative reach.
Exam trap
Moxifloxacin has excellent bioavailability but is never used for UTI — hepatic/biliary clearance means it never reaches therapeutic urine concentrations.
Exam trap
Daptomycin looks perfect for MRSA pneumonia on paper (covers the organism) but is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant — it cannot be used for pneumonia.
Exam trap
Red Man Syndrome (vancomycin) looks like an allergy but is non-IgE histamine release — slow the infusion, don't necessarily abandon the drug.
Exam trap
Ertapenem is a carbapenem ("broadest spectrum" class) but specifically lacks reliable Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, and Enterococcus coverage.
Exam trap
A penicillin/aminopenicillin rash is not automatically a true allergy — the classic exam distractor is the ampicillin + EBV (mono) rash, which is not IgE-mediated.
Exam trap
Clindamycin resistance can be "inducible" and hidden on a routine susceptibility panel — an isolate that looks erythromycin-resistant/clindamycin-susceptible needs a D-test before clindamycin is trusted.
Exam trap
Ceftriaxone should be avoided in neonates — it displaces bilirubin from albumin (kernicterus risk) and can precipitate with calcium (biliary pseudolithiasis).
Exam trap
Cefotetan/cefamandole's MTT side chain causes two seemingly unrelated problems from one mechanism: bleeding (inhibits Vitamin K synthesis) and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
Exam trap
Imipenem's seizure risk is a GABA-receptor competition effect, not a simple "high drug level" phenomenon — renal failure raises the risk because the drug accumulates, but the mechanism is neurochemical.
Exam trap
TMP-SMX in a patient with HIV/AIDS carries a strikingly high (50–80%) rate of hypersensitivity reaction — don't be surprised if a PJP-prophylaxis vignette includes fever and rash.
Exam trap
"Aminoglycoside not working despite correct organism" in a pneumonia or abscess vignette — think poor tissue penetration / acidic, low-oxygen environment impairing active uptake, not necessarily resistance.
Exam trap
Gray baby syndrome is caused by a missing hepatic conjugation enzyme (UDP-glucuronyl transferase) in neonates, not by immature kidneys.
Exam trap
Chloramphenicol has two completely separate bone marrow toxicities — don't conflate the common, dose-dependent, reversible one with the rare, dose-independent, potentially fatal aplastic anemia.

Last-Minute Cram Sheet

Read this in the final 5 minutes. Nothing here is new — it is the distilled version of everything above.

Targets (memory map)

  • Cell wall — beta-lactams (PBP/transpeptidase), vancomycin (D-Ala-D-Ala)
  • Cell membrane — daptomycin
  • 30S ribosome — aminoglycosides (cidal), tetracyclines (static)
  • 50S ribosome — macrolides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, linezolid (mostly static)
  • Folate synthesis — sulfonamides (DHPS) + trimethoprim (DHFR)
  • DNA replication — fluoroquinolones (gyrase / Topo IV)

Beta-lactam essentials

  • Evasion: destroy · change target · keep out · pump out
  • Cephalosporin generation exceptions: ceftazidime & cefepime = Pseudomonas · ceftaroline = MRSA · ceftriaxone = neither
  • Carbapenems = broadest spectrum. Imipenem needs cilastatin. Ertapenem skips Pseudomonas/Acinetobacter/Enterococcus.
  • Aztreonam = Gram-negative only, cross-reacts only with ceftazidime

Glycopeptides

  • Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala. VRE resistance = D-Ala-D-Lac swap.
  • IV vancomycin = systemic. Oral vancomycin = C. difficile only.
  • Red Man Syndrome ≠ allergy (histamine release, slow the infusion).

Protein synthesis inhibitors

  • "Buy AT 30, CELL for 50" — Aminoglycosides/Tetracyclines = 30S; Chloramphenicol/Erythromycin/Linezolid/Lincosamides = 50S
  • Aminoglycosides need O2-dependent uptake → no anaerobes. Once-daily dosing exploits Cmax/MIC + PAE.
  • Clindamycin = best anaerobic + antitoxin coverage, but #1 C. diff risk
  • Chloramphenicol = 3 toxicities: reversible marrow suppression (dose-dependent), aplastic anemia (idiosyncratic), gray baby syndrome (no UDP-glucuronyl transferase)
  • Linezolid = blocks 70S initiation, covers MRSA/VRE, causes thrombocytopenia + serotonin syndrome risk

Antifolates

  • Bacteria must make their own folate; mammals absorb it — that's the whole selective-toxicity story
  • Sulfonamide mimics PABA → blocks DHPS. Trimethoprim mimics folate → blocks DHFR.
  • TMP-SMX = sequential blockade = bactericidal (5:1 ratio); each drug alone is static
  • Toxicity: sulfonamides → SJS/TEN, crystalluria, G6PD hemolysis, kernicterus; trimethoprim → megaloblastic anemia (reverse with folinic acid), hyperkalemia

Fluoroquinolones

  • DNA gyrase (Gram-neg) + Topoisomerase IV (Gram-pos) → double-strand DNA breaks → bactericidal
  • Cation chelation blocks oral absorption (antacids/Ca/Fe/dairy)
  • Moxifloxacin = hepatic clearance, no UTI use. Only cipro/levofloxacin are reliably antipseudomonal.
  • Toxicity: tendon rupture, cartilage damage (avoid <18/pregnancy), aortic dissection, QTc prolongation

Adverse effect patterns

  • Type I hypersensitivity = minutes-1h, IgE, anaphylaxis (penicillins). Type IV = days-weeks, SJS/TEN (sulfonamides).
  • Organ toxicity is Type B/predictable/dose-dependent: nephro (aminoglycosides, vancomycin), oto (aminoglycosides, irreversible), hepato (macrolides, TMP-SMX), neuro (fluoroquinolones, high-dose beta-lactams), hematologic (chloramphenicol, linezolid, sulfonamides)
  • Highest C. diff risk: fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, broad-spectrum beta-lactams

Contraindications to lock in

  • Tetracyclines: pregnancy, <8 years (teeth/bone)
  • Fluoroquinolones: pregnancy, <18 years (cartilage), QTc-prolonging drugs on board
  • Aminoglycosides: myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular blockade)
  • Sulfonamides: near-term pregnancy/neonates (kernicterus)
  • Ceftriaxone: neonates (kernicterus, biliary sludging)

Essential exceptions ("no coverage")

  • Aminoglycosides = no anaerobes · Aztreonam = no Gram+/anaerobes · Vancomycin/linezolid/daptomycin = no Gram-negatives
  • Daptomycin = no pneumonia · Ertapenem = no Pseudomonas/Acinetobacter/Enterococcus · Moxifloxacin/ceftriaxone/ceftaroline = no Pseudomonas · Metronidazole = no aerobes

Practice Questions

The lecture's own sample questions (from the Didactic Study Guide, page 28), reformatted with hidden answers.
Q1. Which of the following agents prevent the formation of bacterial folic acids? ▼
  1. A. Azithromycin
  2. B. Meropenem
  3. C. Ciprofloxacin
  4. D. Sulfamethoxazole
Show answer
Answer: D. Sulfamethoxazole directly blocks folate synthesis by mimicking PABA and inhibiting dihydropteroate synthase.
Q2. Erin, an experienced movie sound editor, was diagnosed with an inner ear infection. Which drug group is rational for Erin? ▼
  1. A. Aminoglycosides
  2. B. Glycopeptides
  3. C. Lincosamides
  4. D. Macrolides
Show answer
Answer: C. Lincosamides (clindamycin) do not carry an ototoxicity risk. Since Erin's career depends on her hearing, this is the safest choice compared to aminoglycosides or glycopeptides (vancomycin), both of which risk ototoxicity.
Q3. Which of the following statements is true of penicillin? ▼
  1. A. Penicillin G is broad spectrum
  2. B. Methicillin is primarily effective against Gram-negative infections
  3. C. Piperacillin is an antipseudomonal penicillin
  4. D. Co-amoxiclav is strongly inhibited by beta-lactamases
Show answer
Answer: C. Piperacillin belongs to the extended-spectrum (antipseudomonal) penicillins, developed specifically to cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Q4. Red Man Syndrome is an adverse effect associated with: ▼
  1. A. Ampicillin
  2. B. Gentamicin
  3. C. Fosfomycin
  4. D. Vancomycin
Show answer
Answer: D. Red Man Syndrome is a rate-related infusion reaction (not a true allergy) caused by rapid IV vancomycin administration, producing flushing, pruritus, and erythema.
Q5. A 35-year-old penicillin-allergic bank president has community-acquired pneumonia. He needs to close a big contract in 6 days and wants to recover in time. He responds well to macrolides. On the basis of affordability, suitability, and safety, which antimicrobial is most rational? ▼
  1. A. Azithromycin
  2. B. Clarithromycin
  3. C. Erythromycin
  4. D. Roxithromycin
Show answer
Answer: A. Azithromycin's long half-life allows a shorter treatment course than the other macrolides listed, fitting his tight timeline while remaining affordable and safe.
